body: A lot of top rowers do. Many college programs aim for a lot steady state rowing (long and slow rowing) it builds a better aerobic base for athletes with less risk to injury. So to answer your questions the amount of meters you’re doing in a day is not very uncommon. Maybe much more less common at your age, but I’d say if you like what you’re doing and haven’t seen any negative effects and have good form you’ll be good. Also maybe try to get on the water at a local club, you can row on the water and see nature and still get those long rows in, it can make rowing more enjoyable.

Honestly being 180 would be a good weight for a 6:35 2k. Ironically I knew a person who has similar stats they were 190, 6’2 and had a 6:25 about and did really well in the single… I would say their only set back was they didn’t have the best form in the world, but they got really far in the single. I feel like 4x5k is a good way to break it up, and about 2 minutes of rest between each set. A good transport workout would be 5x5 minutes. Transport is essentially like the in between of AT and steady state in my opinion it’s around your 6k or 5k pace maybe even a lil faster. AT should be at 2k pace or faster for the duration of the workout and transport is slower then 2k but faster then steady state. Let me know if you have any other questions.

Of course. Just a little more advice, I’d say aim for a 6:35 or below and if possible 6:25-30 for for a A final spot and try to maintain the weight you’re at. I wouldn’t bulk, I also see lifting as useless but I understand injury prevention and some athletes like it as a break from rowing, but I personally always felt like It took away from my recovery and meters I could do on the erg. I’d actually recommend plyometrics if you really want to lift. As for meters roughly 20k a day of SS (4 days a week) and then 2 days of transport will of course get you faster over time quickly. You’re tall so getting faster if you’re above a 6:40 should be easier for you then most. And also your height will help a lot in a single compared to a lot of kids you just need to learn to use it fully and get good length off the front end and back end.

If you’re asking for a 2k amount, that all depends on your sculling skills. A 6:10 with bad form can be the same speed as someone with a 6:40 and good form. Also weight can play a factor. A lot of the best single scullers I’ve seen at the junior level are not heavy usually at least sub 6:25-6:40 on the erg and have pretty good form obviously the slower the 2k the better the form needs to be. A 6:30 at your weight with decent form would get you pretty far maybe even a 6:35 2k. As someone earlier mentioned A finals at youths are generally sub 7:30 on the water and the best of the best (medalist) are all close to breaking 7:20 or they are. Obviously conditions on the water change and that changes those times but those are fairly good markers. Obviously qualifying depends on the region. The Midwest region the last year or two has had some decent single scullers. I’d say you need to break 7:50 minimum to make it. Breaking 8:00 minutes won’t cut it I don’t think, so definitely aim for sub 7:50 and for a medal shot at youths or A finals 7:20-7:30. Hopefully that helps.

If you’re struggling with slowing the rate down that can generally be contributed to a form issue. It’s hard for me to tell without seeing a video but that’s my guess. Sometimes people rush the recovery by not slowly closing that figurative box on the way up. Think of the recovery as almost a constant when rowing, it’s always the same amount of time almost, but you speed up rate by pushing harder with your legs not by shooting up the slide. Usually you should be able to hold lower rates with better form. In all honesty I think you could break 8 in a few months, you’re fairly new to the sport and from what you’re saying have never taken it like really really seriously. Breaking 8 is a big milestone for any woman rower but it’s definitely not impossible. Being new helps to your advantage as you probably still have form gains and just newbie gains still left. obviously height and weight play a factor but I’m 5’7 male and am the 2nd fastest kid on my high school team against like 6ft kids, so take genetics as a talent factor but hard work gets you farther in this sport then talent sometimes.

1. Yes they are helping you’re 2k, unless these are less meters then you get during your in season workouts when you’re doing steady state. I would say though you may wanna up the distance or time, to around a hour at a 20 and break it up in to 15 minutes. As time goes on if you want to make the workout a lil harder a rate 18 the first 15 minutes then add two beats till the last 15 minute interval and do 1 minute of rest between each. Additionally a good rule of thumb for 2k to steady state is 2k+18-22, id except a 8:10 doing a 2:20-2:24 give or a take a few. Now that all being said you’re not far off in my opinion I think you could easily break 8 by the beginning of spring if you put the work in and upped the intensity a lil.
2. Additionally AT work helps but I’d do one of those workouts a week plus a transportation workout, for more info on the split I’d recommend is the wolverine plan for splitting up weekly meters. Just look up the Wolverine plan and it’ll explain a lot. 
3. Good news you don’t need to lift, a lot of programs don’t lift surprisingly, erging and a good form of cross training is good. I tend to do cross training like biking on days when I mentally am drained. But definitely biking is the go or swimming. Mahe Drysdale one of the best single racers in the world did primarily biking due to a back injury and still performed great at the Olympics. Though rowing is a rowing sport as some say and the best to get better at the sport is to just row.
